title: The Body as a Tent and the Mystery of the Incarnation
english: His participation. And his state is his temple, in which God is found, in which God dwells. Perfect virtue is a house of God. 'And Christ as a son upon his house, of which we are the house,' and; 'Do you not know that you are the temple of God?'; except that we have called both virtue and perfect holiness a house, and secondly, faithful men. For this reason they become a house, because they possess virtue and holiness. It is not that the virtue makes the participants a house of God, but because of the virtue do those sharing in it become a house. And that which is over all is written as an end most especially. But because this does not happen all at once, we call the things before the end 'ends'; for there are also ends before the end: 'I have seen the end of all things' (Psalm 37:30). 'When a man has completed, then he begins.' So when he has completed, he sees the end of a certain progress; then, beginning, he seeks to see another end, and over all things he encounters the end that is over all things.

Take for me an example from the construction of a city: he who desires to build a city magnificently and—what more can I say?—royal, begins the construction. He begins to quarry stones. Often the quarrying completes much. When he has prepared those which are needed and as many as are needed, then he begins to seek a place where he will raise up the city. It becomes 'God all in all' (1 Cor 15:28), not all in each one, but 'in all'. In one he is a mourner, when someone hastens to be such; in another a good judge, in another righteous, in another a dispenser of grace, in another as a teacher to a disciple. And in all, indeed, he becomes all things to those who have drawn near to him, but not all things in each one, but either one, or two, or three gifts. And so that we may make this clear regarding the gifts: 'Receive of the Spirit'; one has the word of wisdom, another the word of knowledge, another the gift of healings. But when someone becomes perfect, no longer having the 'earnest of the Spirit' (Eph 1:14), but the Spirit itself, he becomes all things in each one. I become a perfect bearer and a bishop of the temple of God, not having anything else before my eyes except this, the temple of God, seeing it; for he has hidden me in his tent in the day of my evil. For this reason, 'One thing I have asked and this I will seek: that in the day of my evil he has hidden me in his tent' (Psalm 27:8). And progress was being spoken of. Amidst many evils lying ahead and those willing to harm me, he has hidden me. And it is sometimes said...

And the body is a tent; for it is said, 'the earth is a tent for the prudent' (Ps 103:29), and, 'we groan being in the tent' (2 Cor 5:4). Often, while we are still dwelling in the tent, the body hides us so that we are not harmed by it when someone, as I said previously, surrounds the death of Jesus in the body and strikes the body and enslaves it.

'He covered me in the secrecy of his tent.' For the secrecy of his tent is not harmful, but a covering. But the accessible part of the tent, which is already [laid] bare, harms rather. In this way, I am a body dwelling as if not being in a body, being swallowed up of the mortal 'by life.'

To swallow and to swallow up in the Scripture signifies victory; 'in whom they raised [us], therefore we would be swallowing living ones,' instead of 'he conquered us.' And, 'Israel was laid waste, now it has become among the nations like a useless vessel' (Ps 79:6). 'All,' he says, 'who eat him will transgress.' But the eater is being swallowed up. In the tent, therefore, 'in the secrecy of his tent he hid me.'

One who has become in the body is also able, if he perceives the cause and the mystery through which it has happened in him, to be hidden in the secrecy of it; for having immediately known the mystery and the cause, he will harm himself and will not be swallowed up. And this can be said about the Savior or toward the Savior. If regarding him it is said: 'in the secrecy of his tent he hid me,' he had a tent, he became man. The descent of the Savior has a hidden mystery.

He who is able, after the one who became flesh has tabernacled in him, to say: 'we beheld his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth' (John 1:14), was covered 'in the secrecy of his tent.' His covering has become the perceiving of the mystery of the Savior's coming. The Jews, indeed, did not perceive, and as many as are such, and they were not covered 'in the secrecy of his tent.'

And it is possible also, according to the previous argument, for the secrecy of the tent to be the end; for because of this they advance, even if it eludes those who advance; for unless someone reaches it, he is not able to see it as it is, seeing God then 'as he is' (1 John 3:2), when he comes to the end of blessedness. But, have we beheld already? — we certainly do not know. In part...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Commonality of the Righteous and the Rock
english: We know. But is it the human race that says these things? It is not the Lord's man who says these things, but the race of the righteous, the collection of the saints; for even the Son of God does not say according to man, 'The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?' (Ps 27:1). Many times I have said that the things said about the righteous men and about the Lord's man are said in common; but they are common not according to equality, for without comparison he surpasses all even in these things. I say these things are common according to participation, just as I say the medical art is common to the one who has been perfected and holds it without lack, and to those still progressing. I do not say common according to quantity, but according to quality.

The adulterer is not hidden, but goes outside the tent; for he does not abstain from 'the fleshly desires, which wage war against the soul' (Gal 5:17). But he who clearly lives all things according to the flesh—being uncontrolled, living in luxury, and altogether preferring pleasures over the watchful ones, even if they be unendurable—he has his tent manifest, he has the body manifest; it is evident that a body surrounds him. For he who says, 'But you are not in the flesh', teaches being outside the passions of the flesh. But he who is outside the passions of the flesh is hidden in the tent. According to another sense, the tent is a hiding place, not known to all.

'You have raised me in a rock' (Ps 92:14). It is not a great thing to be raised in a sensible rock so as to send up grateful praises. All things happening by God, on which it is fitting to give thanks, which must be praised, are not at hand, nor are they able to be present to everyone. The rock, therefore, is the unshakeable Word of God himself, who, becoming the one around, is not cast down. For it has been said also in others: 'The judges laid hold of a moving rock' or 'their strong [ones]'; and indeed, rulers being outside the rock seem to be strong and to prevail over the uncertain. But when they become near the rock, they are immediately defeated.

And I said also yesterday, that the swallowing up signifies the victory; 'in rising up against us living, they would have swallowed us up', and; 'those swallowing up Israel with their whole mouth' (Ps 83:5). The one being defeated is swallowed up, the one surrounding swallows up. You have, therefore, some enigma having happened in the Exodus, Aaron having thrown his staff according to the guidance of God; and it has become...
the scepter of truth
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Nature of Psalms and Chronology
english: A shout of victory is offered at his tent. The shout signifies victory, for it is a loud cry made against fallen enemies. For instance, when they encircled Jericho and blew the horns and shouted, the walls of Jericho fell at their shout. Jericho, allegorically, is a place on earth, interpreted as the moon; the place on earth is not according to its increase, but according to its decrease, like the fool: for 'fool' means 'as the moon changes.' Therefore, when he encircles his tent according to all interpretations—the progress was called a tent—the one progressing and succeeding truly becomes a circle of it. And again, the body was called a tent. When the inner man resolutely sets himself against the body, he becomes a circle around it and conquers. When anyone encircles the tent, the body of Jesus, through faith, he is proved a conqueror.

6 I will sing and I will play to the Lord (Ps 94:1). It was said to us in the earlier psalms that to sing means to have contemplation, to send up praises and songs without an instrument. It was said that to play means to practically pour out the song of triumph. Both, then, he says, are sufficient for me: I will play and I will sing. I sing by contemplating the truth. He who takes in the dogmas of piety and having contemplation of their scientific and wise nature, sings. But he who, taking the body as an instrument, both a lyre and a psaltery, striking its strings which are all the impulses and the senses, being able to bring forth a psalm harmoniously, that one plays. This, then, is the holy man who is promised to do the two: to sing and to play. He who subdues his body and disciplines it and performs the moral virtues, such as one doing almsgiving, one establishing gentleness, one advancing in courage, he plays. But he who contemplates each mystery of the truth and is able to penetrate with knowledge every dogma of piety, he sings.

Regarding: 'In the fiftieth, as if we receive some confession upon sin?'—obviously it lies there: 'When Nathan came' and rebuked him concerning Uriah (2 Sam 12). It was a time of confession, and the psalm there sends up a confession. After he had reigned and entered to Uriah, that psalm occurred. Here, however, 'before being anointed' is sung, so that also...

This one differs from that one in time and in practice. But how then is one singing? For virtue is unchangeable. Judas neither saw nor sang to the Lord. Those handed over to the Satan, in order that they might be disciplined not to blaspheme, had not possessed a certain dwelling place and progress in faith and virtue.

However, observe that the various psalms are not altogether spoken concerning one and the same person; for this we have said, that they depend on what kind of person is established according to virtue or wickedness. It is not the same thing to say that a man is without sin and to say that a righteous man is without sin. The one possessing righteousness is not able to be made subject to sin; for how could it be, if the opposites do not coexist? The one possessing evil is not able to have good, unless he first turns away from the evil. Look to what kind of person, not to this one or that one; for when I say that the faithful man is able to do all things, I do not say this one or that one, but all things for the one possessing faith. And even if ever, being faithful, someone possesses the power to do all things and succeeds, but the things of faith fall away from him, I do not say that the faithful man does not succeed, but that this specific man does not succeed.

But is the psalm after this one not earlier in time? The psalms do not require such an order as you seek. That psalm is the one rebuking the Syrian, David. King Saul was at his peak and very much in strength when David was slandered and fled. But much later happened the things concerning Uriah, and much later happened his reigning over all after the final anointing—and this was the third. And much later happened the things concerning Uriah. He was not yet reigning when David threw him out as having taken loaves and the sword of Goliath. Not thus, therefore, is the order of the psalms sought according to the order of times, but according to the successes, but according to the events.

The number fifty has something exceptional; and because of its virtues, the psalm of confession was placed upon it. Observe, then: according to the number fifty, repentance is accomplished. Immediately, too, when the Savior was murmuring at the grumbling of the Pharisees concerning the woman cleansed by him and who came to wash his feet with her own tears and to wipe them with her own hair three times, he proposed: 'Two debtors were to a lender; one owed ten drachmas...'
